name: portr
language: Go (server/CLI core), some Python test-server tooling, Svelte admin UI
popularity: 3.2k stars, 115 forks, 10 watchers on GitHub; actively branded product with docs site (portr.dev), YouTube demo videos, and a distributed npx skill package -- moderate-to-good adoption for a self-hosted ngrok alternative.
maturity: 612 commits on main, active development including recent additions (AGENTS.md, Claude/Codex agent skills folder added recently), has tagged GitHub releases and goreleaser config -- appears actively maintained, no obvious red flags.
client_requirements: Single Go binary CLI (portr http/tcp), installed via install.sh or package manager. Works over SSH remote port forwarding under the hood -- no TAP/TUN interface, no root/admin required to run the client on a dev machine.
server_requirements: Full server source available (Go, SQLite + litestream, migrations, Dockerfile/docker-compose). Server setup is Docker Compose or binary; has an admin dashboard for team/user/connection management implying some backend API, but this is primarily a web UI for humans, not a documented public REST API for programmatic tunnel registration by a third-party app.
has_programmable_api: Unclear/likely false as a documented external API -- true only in the sense of an internal HTTP API backing the admin dashboard; no publicized REST API docs for registering tunnels programmatically from an external app like a SvelteKit backend.
viability_notes: Client is admin-free and TUN-free (SSH port-forward based), which satisfies hard constraints, and hosting the Go server binary is reasonable. However there's no clearly documented control-plane/REST API for our SvelteKit app to programmatically register tunnels -- tunnels are driven by CLI/SSH, not an API we'd integrate against, and it's AGPL which may matter for licensing.

name: piko
popularity: 2.2k stars, 87 forks, 12 watchers; positioned explicitly as an open-source Ngrok alternative built for production traffic and Kubernetes hosting -- solid adoption signal for a project this size, with Prometheus/Grafana dashboards and Helm charts included.
maturity: 426 commits, includes Helm charts, benchmark suite, cluster tests, and a wiki -- indicates active, production-oriented maintenance with no obvious red flags (MIT license, structured repo).
client_requirements: Piko agent (`piko agent http/tcp`) or Piko forward (`piko forward`) run as simple CLI/binary processes making outbound-only connections to the Piko server. No TAP/TUN interface and no root/admin required. There is also a Go SDK for embedding a `net.Listener` directly in an application.
server_requirements: Full server source available (Go), designed to run as a cluster of nodes behind a load balancer/Kubernetes Gateway. Has a Prometheus endpoint, access logging, and a documented status/admin API for monitoring; endpoints are registered dynamically by upstream agents connecting -- no static config needed per endpoint.
has_programmable_api: Partial/true -- there is a Go SDK (`piko` Go module) for opening listeners programmatically and a status/observability API, but no TypeScript/JS-native server API; a SvelteKit backend would need to shell out to the Go agent/CLI or hit the Go server's HTTP endpoints rather than use a native JS SDK.
viability_notes: Strong architectural fit: outbound-only, no TUN/root client, hosted Go server binary is fine, and endpoints register dynamically without static config, which is close to a control-plane model. Lacks a native TS/JS SDK, so integration from SvelteKit would go through HTTP/CLI rather than an idiomatic JS library, but is otherwise one of the better fits.

name: gsocket (Global Socket)
popularity: 1.9k stars, 201 forks, 42 watchers; long-running project (the Global Socket Relay Network, GSRN) with active social presence (Telegram, Twitter) and a public free relay service -- reasonably well-known in the security/pentesting community.
maturity: 755 commits, shields.io badges show 'Maintenance: yes' and active build/quality/coverage CI -- actively maintained low-level C toolkit.
client_requirements: gs-netcat and related CLI tools are plain binaries (install.sh or package managers); no TAP/TUN interface and no root required for basic NAT-traversal TCP tunneling use.
server_requirements: No traditional 'server you host' in the tunnel sense -- gsocket relies on the public GSRN relay network (or a self-hosted relay, source available) which just relays encrypted TCP; there is no HTTP control-plane/REST API for registering tunnels. Everything is driven by shared secrets/passwords and CLI flags, not an API.
has_programmable_api: False -- it's a low-level secure TCP rendezvous tool (like netcat), not a tunnel-with-control-plane product; no REST/TS/JS API for tunnel registration.
viability_notes: Client-side constraints are fine (no TUN/root, simple binary), but this is fundamentally a NAT-traversal secure-socket primitive, not an HTTP reverse-tunnel-as-a-service with a control plane. We would have to build our own registration/API/session-management layer entirely from scratch on top of it, which defeats the purpose of adopting an off-the-shelf tunnel tool.

name: Selfhosted Gateway
language: Shell/Makefile glue around Docker Compose, WireGuard, Caddy, NGINX (no custom application code)
popularity: 1.7k stars, 88 forks, 23 watchers -- decent traction as a 'RPoVPN' self-hosted Cloudflare Tunnel/ngrok alternative, has a YouTube setup video and Matrix community channel.
maturity: Only 65 commits -- much smaller/newer project than the others; explicitly states 'No custom code, this project leverages existing battle-tested FOSS components' (WireGuard, Nginx, Caddy), so it is essentially orchestration scripts, not an actively evolving codebase.
client_requirements: CONFIRMED WireGuard-based and requires a TUN interface: the client-side docker-compose service explicitly requires `cap_add: [NET_ADMIN]` to run its embedded WireGuard instance. This is a disqualifying red flag against the hard 'no TAP/TUN, no admin/root' constraint.
server_requirements: Server ('gateway') source is available (bash provisioning scripts + NGINX config, no custom app code/API) -- entirely config-file/Makefile driven (`make gateway`, `make link`). No REST API or programmatic control plane; tunnels are provisioned via CLI/Makefile commands generating docker-compose env files.
server_language: Shell/Bash scripts + NGINX config (no dedicated server application language)
has_programmable_api: False -- explicitly 'no code or APIs, just an ultra generic NGINX config and some short provisioning bash script.'
viability_notes: Disqualified: client requires a WireGuard TUN interface plus NET_ADMIN capability (root-equivalent), violating the hard client constraint, and there is no programmable control-plane API at all -- everything is Makefile/docker-compose driven. Not worth further investigation.

name: Wiredoor
language: TypeScript (server/API + frontend), separate Go-based Wiredoor CLI
popularity: 1.6k stars, 78 forks, 6 watchers; polished docs site (wiredoor.net), Docker Hub image, Helm charts repo, and a separate wiredoor-cli repo -- looks like an actively productized project.
maturity: 540 commits, has CI (GitHub Actions), renovate bot for dependency updates, TERMS.md, security policy, code of conduct -- looks professionally maintained and active.
client_requirements: CONFIRMED WireGuard-based: Client Nodes and Gateway Nodes initiate encrypted WireGuard tunnels to the Wiredoor Server. This implies a TUN/WireGuard interface on the client machine. Gateway Node routing further depends on Linux `iptables` rules. This is a red flag against the 'no TUN/no admin' hard constraint -- the CLI likely needs elevated privileges to set up the WireGuard interface, though exact privilege level per-OS wasn't independently verified beyond the docs' implication.
server_requirements: Full server source available, built with TypeScript/NestJS-style structure (package.json, tsconfig, eslint, jest), NGINX for HTTP routing, includes a web dashboard and CLI. Topics include 'api-server' and 'management-system', suggesting a genuine REST/HTTP control plane for managing nodes/services/domains, which is exactly the kind of TS server API bonus feature we want.
has_programmable_api: Likely true, TypeScript -- the repo is tagged 'api-server' and 'management-system' and ships a web dashboard backed by an API, though the README does not show explicit REST endpoint docs inline (would need to check wiredoor.net/documentation for the API reference to confirm scope).
viability_notes: Best-in-class server-side fit (TypeScript API/control-plane, active project, good docs) but disqualified on the hard client constraint since Client/Gateway Nodes are WireGuard-based and need a TUN interface, likely requiring elevated privileges to configure -- exactly the risk flagged in the task brief. Worth a second look only if Wiredoor ever ships a non-WireGuard/non-privileged client mode.

name: SirTunnel
language: Python (~50-line script) + Caddy (Go) on the server side
popularity: 1.6k stars, 125 forks, 14 watchers -- popular for its extreme minimalism; has multiple community forks (matiboy/SirTunnel, daps94/SirTunnel) adding features like multi-user and stale-tunnel cleanup.
maturity: Only 23 commits -- intentionally frozen/minimal ('I'm unlikely to add many features moving forward' per README); author explicitly points to community forks for more features. Low commit velocity is by design, not neglect, but also means limited ongoing support.
client_requirements: No special client at all -- uses a standard SSH client's remote port forwarding (`ssh -tR ...`). No TAP/TUN interface, no root/admin required, and no custom install needed beyond having an SSH client (already present on virtually all systems).
server_requirements: Server source available: just Caddy (open source Go webserver) + a 50-line Python script (sirtunnel.py) that calls Caddy's built-in JSON admin API to add/remove reverse-proxy routes on the fly. It is effectively config-file-free and stateless -- the 'control plane' is literally Caddy's existing HTTP admin API.
server_language: Python (glue script) driving Caddy's admin API (Caddy itself written in Go)
has_programmable_api: True, indirectly -- Caddy's JSON admin API (typically on :2019) is a genuine HTTP control plane for registering routes/certs programmatically; SirTunnel's Python script is a thin wrapper we could reimplement or call directly from our own glue code (Caddy's admin API is not TS/JS but is easily driven by any HTTP client including SvelteKit).
viability_notes: Excellent client-side fit (nothing but a standard SSH client, zero install, zero privileges) and the server exposes a genuine, well-documented HTTP control plane via Caddy's admin API that we could call directly from SvelteKit to register/manage routes. Main downside is the project's minimalism/low maintenance and that SSH availability/config is still an extra moving part versus a purpose-built client binary.

name: boringproxy
popularity: 1.4k stars, 131 forks, 21 watchers; has a dedicated website (boringproxy.io), sponsor (TakingNames.io) with custom-domain integration, and an active community forum (IndieBits) -- moderate but real adoption for a self-hosted ngrok alternative.
maturity: 377 commits, has a CHANGELOG.md and systemd unit files -- shows ongoing maintenance, though development pace appears to have slowed in recent years relative to newer entrants like piko/portr; no glaring red flags but check recent commit dates before relying on it long-term.
client_requirements: Single Go binary CLI (`boringproxy client -server ... -token ...`), no TAP/TUN interface. Client does not need root/admin -- it's the server that may need `cap_net_bind_service` (or root) to bind ports 80/443, not the client.
server_requirements: Full server source available in Go (api.go, tunnel_manager.go, auth.go, ui_handler.go), includes an admin REST API (api.go) that already backs boringproxy's own web UI for managing tunnels/clients/tokens -- this is the closest thing among these 8 to an existing HTTP control-plane for tunnel management, though it's a Go API, not TS/JS.
has_programmable_api: True, Go -- api.go implements a REST-style HTTP API used internally by boringproxy's own web UI for managing clients, tunnels, and tokens; no official TypeScript/JS SDK, but the API is plain HTTP/JSON so a SvelteKit app could call it directly.
viability_notes: Good overall fit: TUN-free, admin-free simple Go client binary; hosted Go server binary is expected/fine; and it already ships a REST API (api.go) plus web UI that we could call directly from SvelteKit for programmatic tunnel registration. Main gaps are no native TS/JS server library and somewhat slower recent maintenance cadence versus piko or portr.

name: Wiretap
license: See LICENSE.txt (BSD-style, Sandia National Labs open source release)
popularity: 1.1k stars, 46 forks, 14 watchers; developed and published by Sandia National Laboratories (US DOE lab) -- credible institutional backing for a security tool, though smaller community than the others.
maturity: Only 82 commits -- smaller/newer project; has GitHub Actions CI and demo GIFs/docs, reasonably polished for its size, but limited commit history to judge long-term maintenance cadence.
client_requirements: VERIFIED CLAIM DOES NOT APPLY THE WAY EXPECTED: Wiretap's README explicitly states the *Server* role (the unprivileged side, running `wiretap serve`) requires no special privileges and uses a userspace TCP/IP stack (similar to sshuttle) instead of a kernel TUN device. However, Wiretap's *Client* role (which holds the actual WireGuard interfaces) explicitly requires 'WireGuard installed' and 'Privileged access necessary to configure WireGuard interfaces (usually root/admin access)' -- i.e. the TUN/root requirement is very real, just attached to the 'Client' terminology rather than 'Server'. Because Wiretap's naming is inverted from typical usage (Client = privileged/TUN side, Server = unprivileged/no-TUN side), a workable architecture for us would be to run the lightweight unprivileged 'wiretap serve' role on the end-user's local machine (satisfying our no-TUN/no-root requirement) and put the privileged real-WireGuard 'Client' role on our hosted, admin-controlled infrastructure.
server_requirements: Full source available (Go), single static binary, no install needed beyond copying the binary onto the machine and running it. No REST/HTTP control-plane API is documented for programmatic tunnel registration -- configuration and peer/route management is done via the `wiretap` CLI itself (configure/serve/add/status subcommands), not an HTTP API.
has_programmable_api: False -- no documented REST/TS/JS API; all control is via CLI subcommands and generated WireGuard config files, not an HTTP control plane we could hit from SvelteKit.
viability_notes: Only viable if we invert Wiretap's own terminology: put the unprivileged, TUN-free 'wiretap serve' binary on the end-user's local machine, and accept that our hosted infrastructure runs the actual privileged WireGuard peer. This does satisfy the hard client constraint (no TUN/root on the local machine), but there's no HTTP control-plane/API for programmatic registration -- everything is CLI/config-file driven, so integration work would be nontrivial glue code around CLI invocation and WireGuard config generation.
